earlier_scan.source_named: Jordan, David 1980. The phonemes of Prai (36pp, SIL ms); Singnoi, Unchalee 1988. A comparative study of Pray and Mal phonology (Mahidol MA); Malapol 1989 Pray grammar. SEAlang/Mahidol archive unreachable.

new_statements.quote: p. 91: "A syllable is said to be stressed if it is more prominent than the surrounding syllables. In Pray, stress is predictable. It is conditioned by the position of the syllable in the stress group, that is, stress always falls on the last syllable of a stress group." p. 28: "The stress group in Pray may have from one to three syllables, but the majority is monosyllabic. If it has two or more syllables, it has as its nucleus one stressed syllable, which is always the last syllable in the group." p. 34: "A minor syllable functions as a periphery in the stress group. Its occurrence is optional. It bears no stress, and normally occupies the initial position of the stress group, preceding the major syllable."
new_statements.citation: Singnoi, Unchalee. 1988. A comparative study of Pray and Mal phonology. M.A. thesis (Linguistics: Southeast Asian Languages and Linguistics), Mahidol University, Nakhon Pathom. xiv+209 pp.
new_statements.locator: Chapter II 'Pray phonological system', sec. 4.3.2 'Stress', p. 91 (PDF p. 109); and sec. 2 'Stress Group', p. 28 (PDF p. 46); see also sec. 3.2.1-3.2.2 'Major/Minor Syllable', pp. 33-34 (PDF pp. 51-52)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Prai words ('stress groups') are one to three syllables: one obligatory major syllable, optionally preceded by one (rarely two) short-vowel minor syllables such as /si-/, /ka-/, /pa-/. Stress is non-contrastive and falls on the last syllable of the stress group, i.e. the major syllable; minor syllables are never stressed (sesquisyllabic final stress, e.g. [si'ne:] 'mouse', [ka'cay] 'horns', [si lap'phlap] 'butterfly'). Pitch is likewise predictable from syllable shape (level vs. high-falling), so Pray is not tonal, unlike Mal where pitch is phonemic.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None stated for Pray; the thesis distinguishes only stressed (major) vs unstressed (minor) syllables and notes that pitch on a minor syllable is neutral (p. 30). For Mal, by contrast, Filbeck (1976, ch. 9 in Smalley) and Singnoi's summary (p. 93) describe three sentence-level stress degrees (strong/medium/weak).
new_statements.exceptions: None; the only trisyllabic words found ([si lap'phlap] 'butterfly', [si rak'thak] 'a kind of lizard') still carry stress on the final major syllable; a minor syllable 'in rare cases' occurs in medial position (p. 34).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'stress group', the word-sized unit (one major syllable plus optional minor syllables) that functions within the intonation group; no distinction between stress groups by position in the sentence (sec. 2.2, p. 30). Citation-form / elicited data from one main informant plus other Ban Wang Saw speakers.
new_statements.identity_note: Singnoi 1988 describes the Pray dialect of Ban Wang Saw, Chon Daen subdistrict, Chiang Klang district, Nan Province (main informant Praphan Phuteng); Pray = Prai [prt] phai1238 (she treats Pray and Mal as the two main dialects of T'in; Mal is mall1246). Jordan-Diller 2004 note two Prai speech varieties ('R' and 'Y' medial) plus a 'Longhouse' variety; the stress statement is not variety-specific.
